idiom_name: small behaviour-named interfaces (-er) + mandatory doc comments
implementation_notes: Go replaces the documented abstract interface with two mechanisms: a small interface named after the capability as an agent noun (`io.Writer`, a one-or-two-method `ShippingCostReader`), defined in the package that consumes it, and doc comments that begin with the symbol's name and state what the function returns or does - the toolchain publishes them on pkg.go.dev and `go doc`, and Code Review Comments expects every exported name to carry one. Exported-ness is signalled by capitalization, so the interface is literally the exported set: prefer `order.TotalInMinorUnits()` over a generic `order.Get(...)`, keep predicates adjective-like (`IsCancellable`), and never reuse a canonical name (`String`, `Read`, `Close`) with a different meaning. Keep a wide interface next to its implementation only when the package genuinely is one cohesive service and every method belongs to it.
pitfalls: Defining the interface next to the implementation forces every caller to depend on the whole surface; Go convention puts the small interface in the consuming package, where it can name exactly what that client needs.
A doc comment whose first sentence does not start with the declared name, or an exported symbol with no comment at all, breaks `go doc` rendering and leaves the published interface undocumented.

Package-level names leak into every call site (`util.Do`, `common.Handle`); avoid meaningless package names - the kernel's 'calling a global function foo is a shooting offense' applies verbatim to Go packages.
